results.title: Nebius raises on-demand GPU prices by up to 21% | AskGPU
highlights:
# Nebius raises on-demand GPU prices by up to 21%

From October 1, 2026, a Nebius H100 costs $4.50 per GPU-hour on demand instead of $3.85, and a B300 $9.50 instead of $7.85. The RTX PRO 6000 stays at $1.80.

By Saurabh Khatri · Published Oct 18, 2026

Nebius raised the on-demand prices of its NVIDIA B300, B200, H200 and H100 virtual machines on October 1, 2026. Nebius’s compute pricing documentation lists the price of each GPU before and after that date. The increases run from about 17% for the H100 to 21% for the B300.

## What changed

On-demand price per GPU-hour, in US dollars, excluding VAT and other taxes:

| GPU | Before October 1 | From October 1 | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B300 | $7.85 | $9.50 | +21% |
| B200 | $7.15 | $8.50 | +19% |
| H200 | $4.50 | $5.40 | +20% |
| H100 | $3.85 | $4.50 | +17% |
| RTX PRO 6000 | $1.80 | $1.80 | none |

Nebius bills per second, so a partial hour costs a proportional share of these rates. The documentation lists no change for the L40S.

...

## Preemptible prices changed a week later

The October 1 change left the old fixed preemptible prices in place for a week. On October 8, 2026, Nebius moved preemptible GPUs to dynamic spot pricing, so those rates now move with demand. The documentation now shows only a minimum spot price for each GPU, such as “from $0.79” for an H100.

## What to do

If you rent H100s on Nebius by the hour, your bill for the same work went up about 17% on October 1. Nebius’s prices page also says its prices can change at any time. Before you start a long job, compare the new $4.50 rate with other clouds’ on-demand H100 prices, and check whether spot capacity would suit work that can be interrupted.

Nebius on-demand price per GPU-hour, USD excl. tax

1. B300+21% Before$7.85/hr Now$9.50/hr
2. B200+19% Before$7.15/hr Now$8.50/hr
3. H200+20% Before$4.50/hr Now$5.40/hr
4. H100+17% Before$3.85/hr Now$4.50/hr

results.title: Nebius and CoreWeave Lift Nvidia GPU Prices by Up to 21% |  Email Investing
highlights:
Nvidia rental prices are rising even for last-generation H100s. Nebius has posted an October 1, 2026 on-demand card that lifts selected Nvidia GPU-hour rates by 16.9% to 21.0%. CoreWeave said on September 17 that it is still signing compute at higher prices, including short contracts at about $40 million per megawatt of annualized revenue. A landlord can charge more for a chip it does not make only while that chip stays scarce. That is the signal behind Nvidia, and it is the opposite of a capacity glut.

Nebius’s price page, checked on October 2, still prints two columns. On-demand H100 is $3.85 per GPU-hour. The column marked effective October 1 is $4.50. The same split runs through the H200, the B200, and the B300. Reuters reported on September 17 that this was the second pay-as-you-go increase in about three months, with selected Nvidia GPU rates up 17% to 21%. The card on nebius.com/prices matches that range. It does not show every customer already paying the new rate.

...

Four Nvidia rows have a public before and after. GB200 NVL72 and GB300 NVL72 racks are still “contact us” in both columns. RTX PRO 6000 stays at $1.80. L40S “from” rates do not move. The hike lands on the accelerators customers are queued for.

| Nvidia GPU | Prior on-demand column | Announced October 1 card | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HGX H100 | $3.85 | $4.50 | +$0.65, or 16.9% |
| HGX H200 | $4.50 | $5.40 | +$0.90, or 20.0% |
| HGX B200 | $7.15 | $8.50 | +$1.35, or 18.9% |
| HGX B300 | $7.85 | $9.50 | +$1.65, or 21.0% |

Reuters’ “17% to 21%” is this range, with 16.9% rounded up. “Up to 21%” is the B300. The smaller H100 move is the one that changes the reading. Hopper is not the generation Nvidia is leading with. A prior-generation accelerator getting more expensive to rent is not what surplus hardware looks like.

Put the H100 on a bill. Eight GPUs go from $30.80 an hour to $36.00. Over a 720-hour month the list charge goes from $22,176 to $25,920. An 8-GPU B300 box moves from $45,216 to $54,720. Those are walk-up numbers, before tax, storage, or a commitment discount, and they are not invoices.

...

Commitment discounts can run up to 35% below on-demand for large clusters reserved for multiple months. Full discount on the new H100 card is $2.93 an hour, under the old $3.85 list. On the new B300 card it is $6.18, under $7.85. “Up to” is not “everyone gets.” The headline increase is the unreserved rate.

...

CoreWeave did not publish an H100 card. On September 17 it published a contract print. The release, carried on Nasdaq, says that since June 30, 2026, CoreWeave has continued to contract new compute at higher prices. In the third quarter it has signed short-dated contracts of about three to six months, “with pricing of approximately $40 million per megawatt, calculated as annualized revenue divided by power required to service the related clusters.”

...

Neither company publishes how many accelerators sit in a

...

The third public card is Amazon Web Services capacity blocks. They are reservations, not on-demand. Checked on October 2, the AWS tables price an eight-GPU instance and, in parentheses, the rate per accelerator.

In US East the reserved accelerator rates checked on October 2 are $5.191 for an H100 (p5.48xlarge, eight GPUs at $41.528 an instance-hour, Northern Virginia and Ohio), $5.97 for an H200 on p5e in Ohio, $6.865 for an H200 on p5en in Northern Virginia, $12.355 for a B200, and $14.04 for a B300. Tokyo’s p5 H100 rate is $4.720, under Nebius’s new card, so the geography matters. Against the US East reservation, Nebius’s October 1 card is still cheaper: $4.50 versus $5.191, $5.40 versus $5.97 or $6.865, $8.50 versus $12.355, and $9.50 versus $14.04. CoreWeave published no GPU-hour, so it cannot be ranked here. The table is AWS capacity-block pricing.

Effective October 7, AWS says capacity-block rates per accelerator across available regions will be $5.970 on P5, $6.866 on P5e, $7.895 on P5en, $14.208 on P6-B200, and $16.146 on P6-B300, higher in GovCloud. On the US East H100 line, $5.191 to $5.970 is 15.0% on that reservation rate only. The same notice leaves on-demand and Savings Plan prices unchanged.

The products are not the same hour. Nebius on-demand can be started and stopped if the GPUs are free. An AWS capacity block is reserved in advance and paid up front at the rate in force when it is bought. Even with that difference, the hyperscaler’s reserved H100 in US East sits above Nebius’s new list, and Amazon has scheduled the reserved rate higher on October 7 while leaving on-demand unchanged.

...

A glut runs the other way. The owner of empty halls cuts the rate to fill them. Nebius is adding halls and raising the walk-up rate in the same season.

results.title: Nebius just confirmed the price increase we flagged as unconfirmed last week. Its live now. | Devanshu Rajput
highlights:
Nebius just confirmed the price increase we flagged as unconfirmed last week. Its live now.

H100 pricing on Nebius went from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour, confirmed directly against their own pricing page, a 17% increase. H200 rose 20%, from $4.50 to $5.40. B300 climbed 21%, reaching $9.50. This is Nebius's second rate hike since May, when H100 was still priced at $2.95.

According to GetDeploying's pricing tracker, the median on-demand H100 across 40 providers sat at $3.42/GPU-hour as of September 28, up 15% year over year. The same tracker puts hyperscaler pricing at roughly 58% above specialized GPU clouds for the same chip.

Nobody builds a futures market for a commodity that's reliably getting cheaper. CME Group is launching GPU rental price futures on October 5. That alone signals where this market expects prices to go next.

If a provider quoted you a GPU rate more than a few weeks ago, it's worth checking that number again before you plan a budget around it.

results.title: Cloud GPU Price Index — specification
highlights:
## 1. What it measures

The index is the median publicly listed on-demand rental price of one NVIDIA H100 SXM GPU-hour, in US dollars, across the cloud providers GPU Economy reads. It is computed at every hourly scrape and published three ways: the hourly series (2a), a weekly value - the last hourly point of each calendar week, Monday to Sunday, UTC - and a monthly average over a panel fixed before the month (2b). It measures rate cards: what a provider publishes as its price. It does not measure availability, transacted prices, negotiated prices or capacity.

A second series, the base-100 index, measures change: Chain-linked index, base week = 100: each week's link is the geometric mean of week-over-week price ratios over the (provider, region) pairs quoted in both weeks; the index is the cumulative product. A provider or region joining or leaving contributes no ratio and cannot move it. The base week is the week of September 7, 2026.

...

Median of the latest publicly listed on-demand H100 SXM rate of each (provider, region) pair, so a provider listing several regions enters once per region; node-priced offers divided by GPU count; spot and reserved excluded; marketplace floors (Vast.ai, price_scope=marketplace_floor) excluded; quotes listed in any currency other than USD excluded; a week is published only when at least 8 providers contributed.

One quote per (provider, region): the newest listed rate of each pair in the week. A provider that lists several regions enters the median once per region. weighting_check recomputes the same quotes as the median of each provider's own median: a check on what that rule costs, not a second index. A quote count counts rate cards, not GPUs available to book.

Community-cloud and serverless list prices do enter the index (today RunPod Community Cloud and Modal): each is a fixed hourly rate the provider publishes for one H100, not a marketplace floor. The card median elsewhere on the site leaves community capacity out, because it ranks rate cards you can hold; the index measures listed prices. Leaving the one community quote out would have moved each published week by about $0.025.

...

At every hourly scrape: the median of the newest USD on-demand H100 SXM listed rate of each (provider, region), read within the 48 hours before that scrape, marketplace floors excluded; published when at least 8 providers entered, withheld (no value) otherwise. The same rule as the weekly index, applied at each scrape instead of at the end of the week. Since October 1, 2026 each point is computed by the database the moment its scrape is stored and written together with its constituents (every quote, its read time, source URL and row); a point is never rewritten afterwards, and a later scrape cannot change an earlier one. A week's value is its last point rounded to the cent: the 48-hour window of the last scrape of a week lies inside that week, so the two series agree by construction (checked in both series: the week of September 21, 2026 had 26 quotes from 24 providers and closed at $3.7025, published as $3.70). Points before October 1 were backfilled on that day from the stored reads by the same function. File: price-index-hourly.csv; receipts: `/price-index/hourly/YYYY-Www.csv`. The average of these points over a month, over a panel fixed before the month begins, is section 2b.

...

- `not_confirmed_48h`: not read again within 48 hours of the newest scrape (for a closed week: of that week's last scrape)

...

- Panel.

...

- Placement cannot be bought.

results.title: GPU rents doubled to $8.08 an hour while token prices fell — The Founder Gazette
highlights:
Renting a GPU costs roughly twice what it did six months ago. Tunguz, a partner at Theory Ventures, puts the move from $4.40 to $8.08 per GPU-hour.

Over the same period, the price of inference fell. Both things are true, which is what makes the pricing decision awkward.

His explanation is efficiency. Models are getting cheaper to run faster than silicon is getting dearer to rent.

The figures he cites: Claude Opus 5.5 costs 40% less to run than its predecessor, and OpenAI cut the price of one model by 80% in July and another 50% in September.

results.title: Nebius GPU prices rise across the board, up to… · Slicast
highlights:
A I 컴퓨팅 파워 시장에서 주목할 만한 변화가 나타나고 있습니다. 클라우드 제공업체들이 데이터 센터를 계속 확장하고 있음에도 불구하고, 특정 고급 GPU의 임차 가격은 공급 증가에 따라 하락하지 않고 오히려 계속 상승하고 있습니다.

Nebius가 고객들에게 보낸 가격 조정 공지에 따르면, 2026년 10월 1일부터 회사는 여러 온디맨드 GPU 인스턴스의 가격을 약 17%에서 21% 인상할 계획입니다. 제안된 GPU당 시간당 요금은 다음과 같습니다. H100은 3.85달러에서 4.50달러로 인상되고(16.9% 증가), H200은 4.50달러에서 5.40달러로(20% 증가), B200은 7.15달러에서 8.50달러로(18.9% 증가), B300은 7.85달러에서 9.50달러로 인상됩니다(21% 증가).

이 가격 조정은 중요한 신호를 보냅니다. AI 컴퓨팅 수요의 성장 속도가 여전히 고급 GPU, 전력, 데이터 센터 용량이 온라인에 들어오는 속도를 능가할 수 있다는 뜻입니다. 전통적인 클라우드 컴퓨팅과 달리, AI 클라우드 서비스의 핵심 희소 자원은 서버를 넘어 GPU 가용성, 전력 접근, 액체 냉각 시스템, 네트워킹 장비, 고밀도 랙을 지원할 수 있는 데이터 센터를 포함합니다. 어느 하나의 구성 요소라도 병목 현상에 직면하면 새로운 컴퓨팅 파워를 빠르게 배포할 수 없습니다.

Goldman Sachs Technology Conference에서 Nebius 경영진은 회사의 고객 수요에 대한 가시성이 약 18개월에서 24개월 이상으로 연장되었다고 밝혔으며, 일부 고객은 이미 2028년 상반기의 컴퓨팅 용량을 예약하고 있습니다. 회사는 이전에 희소 Blackwell 용량에 대한 가격 테스트를 수행했으며, 이전 최고 가격보다 약 15% 높은 거래 가격과 표준 판매 파이프라인 견적보다 약 20% 높은 거래 가격을 달성했습니다.

Nebius의 가격 인상의 의미는 단순히 GPU 시간당 약 20% 더 높은 요금을 청구할 수 있다는 것뿐만 아니라 AI 컴퓨팅 시장의 수급이 여전히 공급자에게 유리하다는 점을 확인하는 것입니다. 과거 시장의 주요 우려는 수많은 데이터 센터의 동시 출시가 결국 GPU 임차 시장 과잉 공급으로 이어져 잠재적으로 낮은 활용률, 연장된 투자 회수 기간, 그리고 더 높은 가격 가정에 따라 구축된 회사들의 자산 손상을 초래할 수 있다는 것이었습니다. Nebius는 반대의 신호를 보냅니다. 회사는 새로운 B200과 B300 모델뿐만 아니라 몇 년 동안 시장에 있었던 H100과 H200의 가격도 인상하고 있습니다. 이는 수요가 최신 아키텍처를 넘어 확장되고 있으며, 이전 세대 GPU가 모델 미세 조정, 추론, 과학 컴퓨팅, 특정 엔터프라이즈 워크로드에도 여전히 충분한 성능과 비용 효율성을 제공한다는 것을 의미합니다.

...

그러나 온디맨드 가격 인상이 Nebius의 모든 수익을 20%만큼 균일하게 증가시키지는 않을 것입니다. 대규모 고객들은 일반적으로 고정 가격, 최소 구매량, 그리고 새로운 공개 요율에 따라 즉시 가격을 재결정할 수 없는 서비스 조건이 있는 장기 계약에 서명합니다. 이 조정은 Meta와 같은 클라이언트들이 이미 서명한 장기 용량 계약보다는 온디맨드 및 단기 컴퓨팅 계약에 더 직접적으로 영향을 미칩니다.

가격 인상은 또한 NVIDIA 시스템, 네트워킹 장비, 전력, 데이터 센터 건설 비용도 상승할 수 있으므로 비용 전가를 포함할 수 있습니다.

results.title: The Compute Price Nobody Could See · Joshua Davis
highlights:
On August 11, CME Group and Silicon Data, a GPU benchmarking firm backed by the trading house DRW, announced two futures contracts tied to the hourly rental price of Nvidia’s H100 and B200 accelerators. Each contract would represent a month of rent, with trading scheduled to open on October 5 under NYMEX rules. 1 The contracts will now miss that date by at least a month. On September 21, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission informed the exchange that it was extending its review by forty-five days, to November 9. The agency cited what it called “novel or complex” questions, among them the risk that a fragmented and lightly observed rental market could be manipulated.

...

That segment is useful, but it covers a narrow slice of the market. After all, most of the capacity that frontier labs and hyperscale tenants consume moves through multi-year reservations whose terms never appear in any index. Those terms have also behaved differently from the spot market. SemiAnalysis, which launched its own one-year H100 rental index in April, found that one-year contract pricing rose almost 40%, from a low of $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 by March 2026. 6 Over the same months, on-demand capacity sold out across every GPU type, and holders of locked-up instances refused to release them. Silicon Data’s neocloud H100 series, meanwhile, climbed from $2.57 on May 4 to $2.75 on July 27. 7 In August, Bank of America’s semiconductor analyst Vivek Arya described GPU spot rental prices as near all-time highs, citing roughly $2.80 per hour for the H100 and $5.66 for the B200. 8
